lines.text: My name is Ruth, and I grew up in a small flat in Stamford Hill.
There were six of us children, and my mother kept the whole house together.
Every Friday night the table was full: neighbours, cousins, anyone who had nowhere else to go for Shabbat.
My father always said that a home is only as warm as the door is open.
Um, you know, we didn't have much money, but we never felt poor.
When I was twelve my grandmother taught me to light the candles, and I still use her candlesticks today.
Faith for me was never about rules.
It was about belonging to something bigger than yourself, to the generations before you.
After I retired I started volunteering at the food bank.
And that changed my life, honestly. I remember a young mum who came in with her baby and just cried, because someone was kind to her.
That's when I understood what my father meant about the open door.
So, um, my grandchildren come with me now.
I hope they carry it on: the candles, the Friday nights, and helping whoever needs it.
That is the legacy I want to leave, not money, but a full table and an open door.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1
lines.text: Welcome everyone to the concert tonight.

lines.speaker: Speaker 2
lines.text: Thank you all for coming, it means so much to us.

lines.speaker: Speaker 1
lines.text: Please put your hands together.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: So tell me how you first got involved with the youth club.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: I was nineteen and, uh, a friend dragged me along to help with the Sunday football.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: I thought it would be one afternoon. That was thirty years ago.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: The kids who came had nothing to do at the weekend, and some of them had a really hard time at home.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: We gave them somewhere to be, somewhere they were wanted.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: What keeps you volunteering after all this time?

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: Honestly, it's the moment a quiet kid suddenly stands up and leads the team.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: You can see the confidence arrive. I never get tired of that.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: My own school days were hard. I struggled with reading and the teachers gave up on me.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: So I know what it means when one adult believes in you.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: The community here, it's like a second family. When my father died, these kids, now grown up, came to the funeral.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: Forty of them. I couldn't speak. I was so proud and so grateful.

lines.speaker: Interviewer
lines.text: What would you say to someone thinking about giving their time?

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: Just turn up. You don't need to be special. You need to be there, every week, again and again.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: That's what changes a life, not a big gesture, but showing up.

lines.speaker: David Cohen
lines.text: And, you know, you get back far more than you give. I promise you that.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: My parents came to London in 1956 with one suitcase between them.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: They had lost almost everyone in the war, and they didn't talk about it for many years.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: What they did talk about was the future. Education, education, education.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: I was the first in our family to go to university, and my mother cried at the graduation.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: Faith was quiet in our house. Shabbat candles, the prayers my father hummed while shaving.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: When my husband was ill, it was the synagogue community that carried us.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: Meals on the doorstep every night for three months. People I barely knew.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: I learned then that a community is not a building, it's people who notice.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: Um, I suppose, um, I worry sometimes that young people feel alone, you know, on their phones.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: But then I see my granddaughter running the charity bake sale and I have hope.

lines.speaker: Miriam Levy
lines.text: If I could pass on one thing, it would be gratitude. Say thank you, every day.
